anchors.fact: Hugo Ensslin, a German-born bartender who had trained as a painter and photographer before he came to New York at sixteen, worked the bar of a hotel in Times Square. In 1916 he published *Recipes for Mixed Drinks*. It never caught on, and he was never one of the city's celebrated bartenders. One cocktail historian judges that no other book records as exactly what New York's bars were actually serving just before Prohibition.
anchors.meaning: He kept an ordinary season, the drinks people actually ordered, in plain detail. The book never caught on, and that's where his part ends: what lasted is the record, not the man.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me · soughtFor: Honesty · drawnToward: Belonging

anchors.fact: Nobody can say which of the drinks in his book he created. The Aviation's first printed recipe is in it, but the name was already in a newspaper in 1911, and several different drinks shared it.
anchors.meaning: He made nothing up. The keeping was the whole of the work. Never "his drink" or "he invented": the drink is "as his book gave it".
anchors.speaksTo: soughtFor: Honesty · lens: The real me

anchors.fact: The Aviation as his book gives it has gin, lemon, maraschino and two dashes of crème de violette, which tints it a pale sky blue. A far more famous London cocktail book of 1930 printed it without the violette, and that colourless version is the one that survived and was revived. The liqueur itself fell out of cocktail use by the 1930s and was gone from the US for decades. Why the 1930 book left it out is not on record.
anchors.meaning: The famous version lost the colour that was really there. Only the plain record had kept it. That it was "the detail that made it true" is our reading, signposted ("I like to think"). Never say why it was dropped, and never call it careless.
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Beauty · soughtFor: Honesty · texture: Soft

anchors.fact: His book resurfaced in 2003, and in 2007 crème de violette came back to the US. Since then bartenders have split between the version without it and the version with it.
anchors.meaning: The colour came back from the everyday record, not from the famous copy. The return belongs to the record, not to him: no vindication ("finally credited") and no "one day they'll see".
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Wonder · lens: The real me

anchors.fact: His book names a brand of gin, El Bart, in the Aviation recipe, and El Bart was a sponsor of the book. The historian who reprinted the recipe suspects that, rather than taste, is why that gin is named.
anchors.meaning: Even the honest record had an advert in it, and nobody retouched it out. The reason is only a guess, so the reading says "probably".
anchors.speaksTo: lens: My inner child · soughtFor: Honesty · texture: Relaxed

anchors.fact: His book gives two dashes of crème de violette, which one historian reads as about a teaspoon. His full recipe has no sweetener and fails our balance checks, so the glass is a modern build, with a teaspoon of violette put back: the colour is his, the balance isn't. At that dose the drink is a pale sky blue, not purple.
anchors.meaning: Only the colour is his, and it's the part that was really there. Never "made as he made it" or "his recipe". The noticing is the guest's: hold it up to the light.

cocktail.closingLine: Hold it up to the light first. The colour was always there.
cocktail.glassware: a stemmed cocktail glass (a coupe or any small stemmed glass), from the freezer
method: Put a stemmed glass in the freezer.
Pour the gin, lemon juice, syrup and maraschino into a shaker. Add one teaspoon of crème de violette. No more than that.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard for about twelve seconds, until the outside is frosty.
Strain it into the cold glass.
Hand it over while the glass is still frosted.
cocktail.name: As It Was

recipe.item: simple syrup (equal parts sugar and water, stirred until clear)
crème de violette (Rothman & Winter recommended; or any crème de violette, a violet liqueur around 20%)
recipe.note: Ensslin's two dashes, about a teaspoon

cocktail.tagline: You see the moments worth keeping in the days nobody thinks to remember.

reading.epigraph: The truest record of this drink is a book that never caught on.
whoYouAre: "Hold on, don't move," you say, at the kitchen table, on an evening nobody planned. People laugh, because nothing's happening. You know something is: the light across the table, what everyone ordered, the thing someone said that they'll have forgotten by Friday. Other people wait for something worth remembering. You notice it's already here.

Ask you about it and you'll shrug: it's nothing, just a picture. Making a fuss of it would feel like showing off. The shrug covers a fear you don't say out loud: the blur. A whole year going by and looking like one day. Keeping the ordinary is how you make sure it counted. And the people around you get to see their own everyday life the way you saw it: worth keeping.
yours: In 1916, a bartender at a hotel in Times Square published a book of drinks. His name was Hugo Ensslin, and before he came to New York at sixteen he had trained as a painter and, of all things, a photographer. The book never caught on, and he was never one of the city's famous bartenders. But what he wrote down was plain and exact: the drinks New York's bars were really serving, just before Prohibition closed them. One of the best cocktail historians says no other book shows it as faithfully. He even named a brand of gin in a recipe, El Bart, probably because El Bart helped pay for the book. Nobody tidied that out either.

One of the drinks he wrote down was the Aviation: gin, lemon, a cherry liqueur called maraschino, and a violet liqueur called crème de violette, which tints it a pale sky blue. In 1930, a far more famous London cocktail book printed the Aviation without the violette. There's no record of why. But that colourless version is the one that survived. The colour only came back after his book turned up again in 2003, and the violet liqueur returned to America in 2007.

I like to think the violet was the detail that made it true. It wasn't a flourish. It was part of the drink as his book gave it, and it was that plain record that kept it. That's what you do. You don't make things prettier than they are. You keep them as they were, colour, advert and all.

So the cocktail I've made for you has his violet put back: a teaspoon of the violet liqueur, about what his book's two dashes come to. The rest is a modern balance, not his: gin, lemon, a little sugar and a teaspoon of maraschino, shaken and poured into a stemmed glass straight from the freezer. Only the colour is his. It isn't purple. It's a pale sky blue. And many London dry gins carry orris, the root of an iris, whose scent has long been compared to fresh violets, so the violet isn't a stranger in the glass.

One thing I'd ask. Stop calling it nothing. Somewhere in everything you've kept this year there's an ordinary day that someone else has already forgotten. Print it, and give it to the person in it. They don't know yet what their Tuesday looked like. You do.
